newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - S.Africa's slow boat to China - By T.Twine.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - S.Africa's slow boat to China - By T.Twine.

text.p: By Tony Twine, economist at Econometrix financial consultancy

Now that the blow has fallen in the matter of which of the two Chinas South Africa wishes to link with at a diplomatic level, the whole issue seems to revolve more around having one's rice cake and eating it.

When Taipei sent its foreign minister, John Chang, to South Africa within a week of Pretoria's announcement that it was to enter into diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China, at the necessary expense of having to deny the Republic of China similar recognition, this contention jumped crisply into focus.

In the rather rapid flurry of action and reaction over the past two weeks or so -- a remarkably compressed time frame in terms of the time scales of diplomacy -- the vulnerability of Taiwan has been exposed, as has the apparent no-lose position in which South Africa for once has found itself.

When Nelson Mandela announced the policy switch, he did attach a tag which noted that he hoped that trade and aid relations between Taipei and Pretoria would be able to be maintained at the same level that had existed when the two countries had enjoyed ambassadorial links.

One of the first things that Chang put under some doubt was the willingness of his government to maintain the profile of those relations until it knew exactly what South Africa had in mind regarding the interface between the two nations for the future.
Fair enough, but the South African policy makers certainly neither should nor do feel particularly threatened by the blanket of frost which Chang has thrown over the trade and aid landscape.
To quite some extent, Taiwan's suspension of its 36 existing treaties with South Africa, together with aid projects, represents the stamping foot of a butterfly.

The threat that the Taipei government will no longer encourage its citizens to invest in South Africa (notice that this does not yet mean active discouragement, but rather a more passive stance than before) certainly does not come close to resembling economic body blows that would coerce the South Africans into reconsidering their decision to move their diplomatic focus from Tapei to Beijing.

Chang went straight for the hot button when he arrived in South Africa last week to attempt to remonstrate with the authorities here -- and that hot button is investment in South Africa. The Taiwanese have, over the decades, invested in many industries in South Africa. That investment has been in terms of real capital assets, rather than the dominance of financial assets favoured by many of South Africa's large investment partners.

In its own way, this is probably the largest part of the sting to South Africa in Tapei's reaction to being diplomatically dumped. Threats to the physical capital structure of South Africa will elicit rushes of adrenalin from more politicians than any threat to rock the boat in terms of destablising, say, the local bond markets. Closed factories mean losses of jobs, while higher bond yields do not. Not before the next election anyway.

The difficult decision to make the move had already been made before Chang arrived in the country, and there was clearly little that he could do, either in public or in private, to turn the tide. Taiwan probably needs its trade with South Africa as much as South Africa does, if not more so. Taiwan's substantial modern industrial base and its relatively cheap skilled labour requires primary raw material and semi-manufactured inputs to make it work, and few single economies can provide either the variety or the quantity that leaves the ports of South Africa.

Pretoria, on the other hand, will have its eye on the export potential to the PRC, the fourth largest economy in the world. It is the largest single economy, in fact, when measured by purchasing power parity, rather than market dollars.

And then there is Hong Kong, the already cut and polished jewel soon to be added into the PRC economic treasure chest, not to mention other Pacific Rim countries and markets that can be influenced by a word from the authorities in Beijing.

The reality of the real politik is that there is very little that Taiwan can do about the South African decision. That will hurt the pride of the government in Taipei, where South Africa was the largest economy to be represented on a diplomatic level. During the next 12 months, the ROC will doubtlessly learn to grimace and bare the new disposition, and hope that the new policy of South Africa has not caused its rather meagre web of international relations to begin to unravel -- one hears rumours that Venezuela, the next largest diplomatic partner with Taiwan, may also now reconsider its position.

Within its own cobwebs of sometimes enigmatic, and sometimes downright crazy, foreign affairs, Pretoria seems to have an overwhelming weight of economic commonsense behind this decision. What is more, from their own particular foreign relations standpoint, the Africans are forced to support it as well. That makes quite a change.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.) REUTER
